title: Firing into a crowd: a constitutional violation, immunity anyway, and a Bane Act question for the California Supreme Court
summary: One published Ninth Circuit force opinion this week, and it is a teaching case. In Johnson v. Adgar, filed November 2, a split panel held that a San Jose officer who fired a 40mm foam baton round indiscriminately into a retreating protest crowd used excessive force, then granted him qualified immunity because no earlier case squarely covered a mixed crowd that had thrown objects at police. The same panel sent a question to the California Supreme Court about the Bane Act, the state civil rights statute, that could leave California officers exposed under state law even when they win federal immunity. It pairs with Astorga v. Villanueva, the supervisory liability memorandum covered in full in the October 25 brief. No Supreme Court merits decision and no published California force decision were found.
coverage: Checked: the Ninth Circuit's published opinions through the government's official opinion database, which carried the Johnson v. Adgar opinion in full. The companion certification order was not available there and was not read; the certified question is quoted from the court's own summary filed with the opinion.
The Ninth Circuit's own website was serving an expired security certificate on November 8 and could not be read safely.

No Supreme Court merits decision on police force was found for the week, and the October order lists were not reread line by line. References were seen to an Eleventh Circuit qualified immunity decision on a refusal of medical care and to a Nevada baton case, but their filing dates could not be confirmed, so they are not covered.
Unpublished circuit memoranda and the state high courts in Washington and Oregon were not screened exhaustively. Something may have been filed that was missed.

sections.heading: Ninth Circuit
sections.note: One published opinion, with a partial dissent and a companion certification order. Read it next to Astorga v. Villanueva, the unpublished October 21 memorandum covered in full in the October 25 brief: there the Ninth Circuit granted former Sheriff Villanueva qualified immunity on a supervisory liability theory over less lethal munitions at a 2020 protest, because no earlier case put a supervisor who was not on scene and ratified nothing on notice. Johnson is the analysis for the officer at the trigger; Astorga is the analysis for the command staff above him.

cases.name: Johnson v. Adgar
cases.court: Ninth Circuit (from the Northern District of California, Judge Beth Labson Freeman)
cases.topic: Less lethal launcher fired into a crowd, seizure of an unintended target, qualified immunity after a jury verdict
cases.caution: The opinion was read in full from the official database. The companion order certifying the Bane Act question to the California Supreme Court was not read; the question is quoted from the court staff summary filed with the opinion. Verify every quotation against the slip opinion before using it in a report or in testimony.
cases.facts: San Jose, May 30, 2020, the evening after a night of protests one officer called the most violent and destructive he had seen in fifteen years. A crowd at the City Hall plaza had been generally benign through the day, chanting and singing in front of a police skirmish line. Kyle Johnson arrived at 9:53 p.m. with no sign, no weapon, and nothing to throw, and never engaged with the police. Officer James Adgar arrived at 10:13 p.m. with a 40mm projectile impact weapon, which fires a foam baton round the court described as able to cause serious injury or death. He was posted behind the skirmish line and ordered to shoot anyone he saw throwing bottles. At 10:24 p.m. some protesters threw bottles, some of them glass, at the officers. Officers, including Adgar, fired their launchers and the crowd, including Johnson, retreated, then quickly returned. At 10:33 p.m. a second volley was thrown and officers fired again. Johnson, who had thrown nothing, was hit in the back of his left leg. Doctors later diagnosed a pulmonary embolism attributed to the leg injury. The parties agreed Adgar did not intentionally target Johnson. A jury found for Johnson against Adgar on every claim, found for the City on every claim, awarded $1,353,313 in a single undivided sum, and specifically found that Adgar fired indiscriminately into the crowd. The district court denied Adgar's post-verdict motion for judgment as a matter of law on the Fourth Amendment claims.
cases.holding: Reversed in part, vacated, and remanded, in an opinion by Judge Tallman. First, Johnson was seized. Under Nelson v. City of Davis, a person in a group that officers intentionally fire into is seized when the round limits his movement, even though no one aimed at him. Video showed Johnson running, then limping to cover behind a low wall, and Adgar admitted he fired on purpose. Adgar's innocent bystander argument, that he aimed at a bottle thrower and missed, depended on his version of the facts, and the jury's version controls when substantial evidence supports it. Adgar testified he tried to aim at an individual and pulled the trigger once he believed he had identified him, and could not see whether he hit his target; the jury could reasonably find he never had a clear target and shot in the general direction of the thrower. Second, the force was unreasonable. Johnson was committing no crime, posed no threat, and was not resisting or fleeing arrest, since no one was being arrested. The crowd he was in was retreating and contained at most two bad actors. Given the disproportionate number of peaceful people in the part of the crowd Adgar fired into, there was a significant risk of hitting someone not engaged in wrongdoing with a weapon that could cause serious injury or death. The court said the government's legitimate interest in disabling an aggressor is not reasonably served by firing indiscriminately into a crowd and hoping to hit him. Third, the law was not clearly established, so Adgar gets qualified immunity. The parties agreed Nelson was the relevant precedent. In Nelson the group fired on was entirely peaceful, isolated in a narrow breezeway, and had thrown nothing. Here hostile actors had repeatedly thrown objects, two of them were in the part of the crowd Adgar fired into, that part was not physically isolated, and Adgar fired after a second volley, which suggested the throwers could reload and return. The court relied on its 2024 decision in Puente v. City of Phoenix, where a protester hit while walking away from a mixed crowd lost on the same ground, and described Sanderlin v. Dwyer, where an officer deliberately shot a peaceful man holding a sign, as less relevant. It cited the Supreme Court's repeated warning, including Kisela v. Hughes, that precedent must squarely govern the specific facts.
cases.dissent: Judge Paez agreed there was a constitutional violation but would have denied immunity. He wrote that Nelson clearly established the unlawfulness of shooting a projectile weapon capable of causing serious and permanent injury indiscriminately into a group of protesters who did not pose an imminent risk to public safety. He said the majority viewed the evidence in the light favorable to the officer instead of the jury's winner. The evidence about where the bottles came from was at best mixed: a video forensic expert placed the throwers relatively far from Johnson, and Johnson saw no one near him throw anything. He also wrote that the majority could not use Puente, decided four years after the shooting, to say the law was unclear in 2020, and that the majority had reversed the logic of Tan Lam v. City of Los Banos, which allows later cases that found a violation of clearly established law to be considered, not later cases that found immunity.
cases.notDecided: The Bane Act claim. The panel held that a Bane Act claim has the same elements as a section 1983 claim plus specific intent, so the constitutional violation it found carries over, but it did not decide whether Adgar violated a clearly delineated and plainly applicable right under state law. It certified that question to the California Supreme Court, told the district court not to recalculate attorney fees until the panel decides the state claim, and held the mandate. The jury's battery and negligence verdicts were not challenged on appeal.
cases.inPractice: A launcher round that hits the wrong person is not an accident outside the Fourth Amendment. If the officer fired on purpose at a group, everyone in the group is an object of that force. The jury's finding that the fire was indiscriminate decided this case, and the court said it did not matter that Adgar had been ordered to shoot only bottle throwers if the jury could find he did not follow that order. The officer won immunity only because no earlier case involved a crowd that had itself thrown objects at police. That protection is gone for the next Ninth Circuit officer who fires a launcher into a mixed, retreating crowd, because this opinion is now the case on point. In California, a federal immunity win may not end the exposure if the California Supreme Court reads the Bane Act standard differently.
cases.trainIt: Teach the 40mm launcher as a point target tool, never an area tool. The articulation for every round is a named person doing a specific act, the distance, the expected point of impact, and who is behind and beside the target. If the operator cannot identify the target, the operator holds. Use a spotter or team leader to designate the target out loud before the launch, which separates the decision from the trigger and creates a record. Train that a second volley from a few people is not a blank check for area fire at everyone; it helped this officer on notice, not on reasonableness. Train supervisors to document the whole picture, including the hours of peaceful protest, the skirmish line, and the composition of the crowd, because the totality is the test. For command staff: a policy that leans on qualified immunity is written for the lawyers, not the street. Train to the first prong. Review less lethal policy language so impact launchers are separated from area effect dispersal tools, and brief the city attorney and risk manager on the Bane Act certification now.

sections.heading: Supreme Court
sections.note: No merits decision on police force was found this week. The Johnson panel relied on a 2026 per curiam decision, Zorn v. Linton, for the rule that courts generally need a case where an officer acting under similar circumstances was held to have violated the Constitution, and on the Court's repeated specificity warning in Kisela v. Hughes. The October order lists were not reread line by line for this brief.

sections.heading: California
sections.note: No published California force decision was found this week. The California item is the question the Ninth Circuit sent to the California Supreme Court in Johnson v. Adgar. The Tom Bane Civil Rights Act, Civil Code section 52.1, gives a state remedy when someone interferes with constitutional rights by threat, intimidation, or coercion. Under Cornell v. City and County of San Francisco, a 2017 Court of Appeal decision, the right must be clearly delineated and plainly applicable under the circumstances. The certified question, as stated in the court's summary, is: what is the standard for determining whether a particular constitutional right is clearly delineated and plainly applicable under the Bane Act, and what is the difference, if any, between that standard and the clearly established standard for federal qualified immunity. If the answer is that the state standard is different, a California officer could win federal immunity, as Adgar did, and still face state liability for the same force. As of this brief there is no indication the California Supreme Court has acted on the request; it decides whether to accept certified questions, and timing estimates in legal commentary are estimates, not deadlines.

applications.title: Aim at a person, not at a crowd
applications.body: The key fact in Johnson was not that bottles were thrown. It was the jury's finding that the officer fired indiscriminately. Teach the 40mm launcher as a point target tool: if the operator cannot name the person and the act that justify this round, there is no articulation.

applications.title: Designate the target before the launch
applications.body: Use a spotter or team leader to call the target out loud, check the backdrop, and hold fire when the line of fire includes people who have done nothing. That separates the decision from the trigger and creates the record a jury will believe.

applications.title: A second volley is not a blank check
applications.body: The majority gave the second volley weight on notice, which is a legal question about what earlier cases said. It did nothing to make the force reasonable. Do not teach that repeated throwing by a few people authorizes area fire at everyone.

applications.title: Train to the first prong
applications.body: The court held the force unconstitutional. The officer won only because no earlier case was specific enough, and this opinion is now that case for the Ninth Circuit. Qualified immunity is a defense in court, not a tactic on the street, and a policy that cites it is written for the lawyers.

applications.title: In California, brief counsel on the Bane Act certification now
applications.body: If the California Supreme Court says the state standard differs from federal qualified immunity, a federal immunity win will not end the exposure. Ask counsel whether policies and training records are organized to meet a state standard that may turn out to be stricter.

applications.title: Command staff, keep the paper
applications.body: Astorga v. Villanueva, covered October 25, shows that liability at the top of the chain is hard for a plaintiff to prove, and that the record of authorization, supervision, complaint handling, and after-action review is what gets tested. Document those decisions as they are made, and never announce that nobody will be disciplined.

quiz.q: In Johnson v. Adgar, why was Johnson seized even though the officer did not aim at him?
options: Because any injury caused by police is a seizure
Because the officer intentionally fired into a group Johnson was part of and the round limited his movement
Because the officer was ordered to fire
quiz.teach: Under Nelson v. City of Davis, a person in a group that officers deliberately fire into is an object of that force. The jury found the fire was indiscriminate, and the jury's reasonable reading of the evidence controls after a verdict.

quiz.q: Why did Officer Adgar still get qualified immunity?
options: The court found the force reasonable
The jury's verdict was set aside as unsupported
No earlier case squarely covered firing into a mixed crowd that had itself thrown objects at police
quiz.teach: The court held the force unconstitutional. Immunity turned only on notice: Nelson involved an entirely peaceful, isolated group, and the court treated that difference as material. Orders did not matter once the jury could find he did not follow them.

quiz.q: What question did the Ninth Circuit send to the California Supreme Court?
options: Whether 40mm launchers may be used at protests
Whether qualified immunity applies to all state law claims
What standard decides whether a right is clearly delineated and plainly applicable under the Bane Act, and how it differs from the federal clearly established test
Whether the jury's damages award was excessive
quiz.teach: The Bane Act, Civil Code section 52.1, is the state civil rights remedy. If its standard differs from federal qualified immunity, an officer can win the federal claim and still face state liability for the same force.
